transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-08-28
- Time: 16:00 PT
- Duration: 47 minutes (recorded)
- Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Sam (Redwood Product), Jordan (NovaDocs Eng), Maya (NovaDocs PM), Chris (NovaDocs Infra), Taylor (NovaDocs Security)

Summary (auto): Quick migration demo focused on parity mapping from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to Redwood. Covered API shapes, function/tool-calling differences, streaming behavior, embeddings and vector sizes, and security/compliance concerns.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining - Alex Martin from Redwood here, I'm the AE on this account. Quick intro round?
[00:07] Jordan: Hi, Jordan Lee, senior eng at NovaDocs, we own the ingestion and QA pipelines.
[00:11] Maya: Maya Rivera, product. We're looking at migrating chat & summarization flows off OpenAI and some Antropic stuff.
[00:16] Chris: Chris Patel, infra - mainly here for latency/cost and VPC questions.
[00:20] Taylor: Taylor Nguyen, security - SOC2 questions and SSO.
[00:24] Priya: Priya Shah, SE at Redwood, I will run through the technical parity mapping and demo.
[00:28] Alex: Cool, our plan is a short overview then Priya will demo API parity and console. We'll hit Optimize suggestions too.

[00:45] Priya: Alright jumping in - first slide, high level: Redwood exposes a single REST/SDK surface for generation, chat, embeddings, and reranking. We map OpenAI/Anthropic/Together primitives to Redwood models and flags.
[00:58] Priya: For example, OpenAI chat-completions map to Redwood's chat endpoints - function/tool calling is supported but there are slight differences in how tool schemas are validated and streaming events are emitted.
[01:12] Jordan: Can you show that? Our product heavily uses tool-calling to run retrieval and call internal microservices.

[01:18] Priya: Yep - demo time.

[01:22] Priya: (screen share) Here's a sample curl to call the Redwood chat endpoint, note the model param (redwood-chat-medium) and call to tools array. If you were using OpenAI you'd pass messages + functions, in Redwood it's conceptually similar but the tool schema supports richer response routing.
[01:37] Priya: Streaming: Redwood supports SSE and chunked streams; we stream role tokens plus tool-invocation events. Small quirk - the framing token for tool calls is slightly different, so client parsers may need a small adapt layer.
[01:52] Maya: So we'll need to update our client libs? We're using a thin wrapper now.
[01:56] Priya: Typically a few lines. We provide sample adapters in the repo and a parity mapping table that shows exact key changes.
[02:05] Alex: We'll put the adapter snippets in the parity doc.

[02:12] Priya: Next, embeddings - Redwood can ingest OpenAI/Anthropic-sized embeddings. We support 1536, 1024 and custom quantized vectors depending on model. When mapping from Together embeddings you'll want to watch tokenization differences and normalization before storing vectors.
[02:30] Jordan: We run 1536 for semantic search; is there a drop in quality moving to Redwood models?
[02:36] Priya: We maintain parity for curated models in our catalog. For a direct swap we recommend a small re-embedding sample and nearest-neighbor recall check. Usually numbers are within noise but we'll run a quick eval on your seed prompts.

[02:53] Chris: Latency and cost - our SLA target is p95 < 400ms for short queries, and cost per 1k tokens needs to be comparable to OpenAI. How are you seeing that?
[03:05] Priya: On hosted we can hit similar latency depending on model size; for stricter p95 we'd recommend Redwood Dedicated which gives predictable throughput and reserved pools - avoids noisy neighbors. Cost-wise Optimize suggests quantization or batching to drop per-token cost, and we can model your traffic to show savings.
[03:25] Chris: What's K-V cache behavior? We rely on long context caching for conversation state.
[03:30] Priya: We have automatic prefix/KV caching; the runtime keeps KV caches on GPU for active sessions to reduce compute. Note: sometimes docs transcriber says K-V cash, but it's K-V cache. You should see significant recurring token savings.

[03:45] Maya: Any differences in prompt engineering? We have prompt templates with dynamic metadata.
[03:50] Priya: None major - Redwood supports prompt templates, structured output with schema enforcement, and function responses. We also have the Optimize module which recommends batch sizes and quant profiles for your workload.

[04:05] Priya: Now switching to Console - (screen) this is the per-route dashboard. You can see token costs, latency breakdowns, and trace samples. For migrations it's useful to run a side-by-side route on OpenAI + Redwood and compare.
[04:20] Jordan: Can we capture sampling/temperature differences? Our tests rely on identical RNG seeds sometimes.
[04:26] Priya: RNG determinism varies across backends; we provide a 'closest-behavior' mapping and a regression testing harness in the evals repo. For deterministic tests we recommend using embeddings or logits-level comparisons rather than raw string equality.

[04:40] Alex: Quick callout on authentication - Redwood supports API keys, SSO/SAML, and customer-managed KMS for Private deployments. Taylor you had specific SSO questions?
[04:51] Taylor: Yes, we need SAML + SCIM for user provisioning, and proof of SOC2 type II. Also KMS/HSM for encryption at rest.
[04:58] Alex: We have SOC2 docs and can share them; for Private we support customer KMS and HSM integrations. I'll send the security pack.

[05:12] Priya: Back to mapping: Together's completion params sometimes differ in temperature defaults and stop-seq semantics. In the parity doc we list field-level remaps like stop_sequences -> stop, top_p -> nucleus. Also differences in token counting - we include a tokenizer compatibility note.
[05:30] Jordan: Token counting has bitten us - billing spikes vs OpenAI. How accurate is Redwood's token counter relative to OpenAI?
[05:36] Priya: We use the same tokenization heuristics for common models and include a tokenizer library you can run locally for exact counting. There can be small deltas but we surface them in the console cost breakdown.

[05:50] Priya: Demo: function calling flow. I'll call a toy retrieval tool - you can see the tool invocation event streamed, then the tool result pushed back and final response assembled.
[06:03] (short crosstalk, network noise)
[06:10] Priya: Apologies, my network had a small stutter. Continuing - on the client side you'll handle the tool event and call your microservice; Redwood's SDK samples show this.

[06:25] Maya: For our legacy clients, we can't break event sequences. How do you support gradual rollout?
[06:30] Alex: You can run a canary route and do A/B via routing policies. Redwood supports traffic split by percent and auto-fallback to OpenAI or another variant if you see regressions.

[06:43] Chris: For Dedicated, what's the minimum commit? We need cost numbers for finance.
[06:49] Alex: Typical reserved pools start at X GPUs for predictable throughput - I'll include a pricing appendix in the parity doc. There's also burst capacity if you need short spikes.

[07:02] Jordan: Regarding embeddings store, our vector DB is self-hosted. Any gotchas exporting vectors?
[07:08] Priya: Watch normalization and dimensionality. If you re-embed, we recommend a small migration script that re-indexes in batches; Optimize can suggest batching and quantization for storage.

[07:20] Priya: Security again - logs, auditability: Console has per-request audit logs and you can export to SIEM or S3. For Private you get full control plane visibility.

[07:32] Taylor: Does Redwood provide pen-test reports?
[07:35] Alex: Yes, and we can share a security pack with SOC2, pen test summary, and architecture notes.

[07:44] Priya: Now a deeper technical note - model families: we map OpenAI's gpt-x style to our redwood-chat family; Anthropic's Claude-style maps too but with a different safety wrapper. For Together models, we advise specific tokenization and quant profiles.

[08:05] Priya: For their migration specifically, the key risk areas are: 1) function-calling framing differences, 2) tokenization/billing deltas, 3) embedding dimensional parity. Mitigations: adapters, re-embed sample set, and short benchmark run.

[08:25] Jordan: Could you run a sample benchmark with our sample prompts? We need latency and recall numbers.
[08:29] Priya: Yes - we'll request the prompt pack and run on Redwood hosted first, then propose Dedicated if latency needs it.

[08:36] Alex: Homework items we'll capture in an email: parity spreadsheet, adapter snippets, pricing appendix, security pack.

[20:00] Priya: (deep dive) When you stream tokens, Redwood emits role chunks and a tool invocation envelope. Some early clients had to tweak their SSE parser because Redwood includes a small metadata prefix for trace ids.
[20:20] Jordan: Noted. Our client lib uses eventsource polyfill so we'll test.

[24:10] Priya: On batching: Redwood's runtime supports continuous batching and autoscaling. For chat-heavy workloads with many short contexts, small batch sizes maintain latency and still get token savings via KV cache. Optimize will recommend a batch window.

[29:00] Chris: For GDPR/data residency - we host in us-west, but need eu residency for some customers. Is that available?
[29:08] Alex: Yes, regional hosting available on hosted; Dedicated can be provisioned in specific regions and Private obviously runs in your VPC.

[31:15] Maya: Any migration stories from companies using Together?
[31:20] Priya: We have a playbook - common pattern is run a two-week shadow test, compare recall/misinfo, then a canary for 5-10% traffic. We surface regressions via the evals harness.

[35:40] Jordan: A nit - tool calling schema validation, do you do strict JSON schema validation server-side?
[35:46] Priya: We validate schemas and provide warnings; you can choose strict or permissive modes. Strict mode rejects mismatched tool outputs which helps catch production issues earlier.

[39:10] Taylor: For encryption at rest and transit, please confirm TLS and KMS integration options.
[39:16] Alex: TLS in transit is standard; for rest, for Private we integrate with customer KMS/HSM, hosted can use BYOK patterns. We'll put that in the security pack.

[41:50] Priya: Demo wrap-up: parity table includes endpoint mapping, param remaps, sample adapter snippets, streaming caveats, and embedding notes. We'll share a CSV and an example migration script.

[44:05] Alex: Next steps recap?
[44:09] Jordan: We'll deliver the prompt set and traffic profile by 2026-09-01.
[44:13] Priya: We'll run a hosted benchmark and share results, and Alex will send the parity mapping and security docs.
[44:21] Maya: If the benchmark looks good, schedule Dedicated scoping.

[44:30] Alex: Great, thanks everyone - we'll follow up with the parity doc and links.
[44:35] Jordan: Thanks, bye.
[44:37] Maya: Bye.

(End of recording)
